notes:
Faraday's & Lenz's Laws

  • Magnetic flux: $\phi = BA\cos\theta$; induced emf $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$ (Faraday's law); for $N$ turns, $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$.
  • Lenz's law: induced current opposes the change in flux that produces it — a statement of conservation of energy.

Motional EMF

  • Rod of length $l$ moving with velocity $v$ perpendicular to field $B$: $\varepsilon = Bvl$; induced current $I=Bvl/R$; force needed to keep rod moving at constant $v$: $F = BIl = B^2l^2v/R$; power delivered = power dissipated $= B^2l^2v^2/R$.
  • Rotating rod/disc of length $l$, angular speed $\omega$: $\varepsilon = \dfrac12B\omega l^2$.

Self and Mutual Inductance

  • Self-induced emf: $\varepsilon = -L\dfrac{dI}{dt}$; energy stored $U=\dfrac12LI^2$.
  • Solenoid: $L = \mu_0n^2Al = \mu_0N^2A/l$ (n = turns/length).
  • Mutual inductance: $\varepsilon_2 = -M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt}$; for two solenoids, $M = \mu_0n_1n_2A l$ (coaxial, same length/area).
  • Series inductors (no coupling): $L=L_1+L_2$; combining coefficient of coupling $k=M/\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, $0\le k\le1$.

AC Generator

  • Coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, rotating with angular speed $\omega$ in field $B$: $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, where $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega$.
  • Converts mechanical energy to electrical energy; based on Faraday's law of EM induction.

Eddy Currents

  • Induced circulating currents in bulk conductors due to changing flux; cause heating losses (reduced in transformer/motor cores by laminating with thin insulated sheets); used usefully in induction furnaces, electromagnetic braking, and speedometers.

Key Comparisons

EffectCause
Motional emfconductor moving in a field (magnetic force on free charges)
Faraday emf (stationary conductor)changing $B$ in time — induced non-electrostatic electric field

Exam tip

KCET sets around 2–3 questions here: a Faraday's-law flux-change numerical, a motional emf/rod-on-rails problem, and one on self/mutual inductance formula or Lenz's law direction. The rod-on-rails ($F=B^2l^2v/R$) is a favourite recurring numerical.

questions.q: The magnetic flux through a coil of 100 turns changes from 0.02 Wb to 0.06 Wb in 0.4 s. The induced emf is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon = N\Delta\phi/\Delta t = 100\times(0.06-0.02)/0.4 = 100\times0.1 = 10$ V.
questions.trick: $\varepsilon=N\Delta\phi/\Delta t$ — multiply by turns, use the flux CHANGE not final value.

questions.q: A conducting rod of length 0.5 m moves with a velocity of 4 m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. The emf induced across its ends is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon = Bvl = 0.4\times4\times0.5 = 0.8$ V.
questions.trick: Motional emf: $\varepsilon=Bvl$ — straight multiplication, no angle needed here.

questions.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
questions.explanation: The induced effect opposes the cause producing it; if it aided the cause, energy would be created from nothing, violating energy conservation.
questions.trick: Lenz's law = energy conservation; aiding the change would create energy from nothing.

questions.q: A metal rod of length $l$ and resistance-free rails form a circuit of total resistance $R$ in a field $B$. The rod moves with constant velocity $v$ perpendicular to $B$. The force required to keep the rod moving at constant velocity is
questions.explanation: Induced current $I = Bvl/R$; opposing force on rod $F=BIl = B^2l^2v/R$, which an external agent must supply to maintain constant $v$.
questions.trick: Rod-on-rails: force to sustain constant $v$ is always $B^2l^2v/R$ — memorise this formula.

questions.q: A metal rod of length $l=1$ m slides at constant velocity $v=2$ m/s on resistance-free rails (total circuit resistance $R=2\,\Omega$) in a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5$ T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The power delivered by the external agent to keep the rod moving at this constant velocity is
questions.explanation: $P = F v = (B^2l^2v/R)\times v = B^2l^2v^2/R = 0.25\times1\times4/2 = 0.5$ W, equal to $I^2R$ dissipated.
questions.trick: Power by external agent = power dissipated = $B^2l^2v^2/R$ — extra factor of $v$ over force.

questions.q: The self-inductance of a solenoid with 500 turns, length 1 m and cross-sectional area $1\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$ (air core) is approximately
questions.explanation: $L = \mu_0N^2A/l = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times500^2\times10^{-3}/1 = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times2.5\times10^5\times10^{-3} = 10\pi\times10^{-5} \approx 3.14\times10^{-4}$ H.
questions.trick: Solenoid inductance $L=\mu_0N^2A/l$ — turns are SQUARED, easy to miss.

questions.q: The energy stored in an inductor of 2 H carrying a current of 5 A is
questions.explanation: $U = \dfrac12LI^2 = \dfrac12\times2\times25 = 25$ J.
questions.trick: $U=\frac12LI^2$ — same $\frac12$ pattern as capacitor and kinetic energy.

questions.q: An ac generator coil of 100 turns, area 0.1 m$^2$, rotates at 50 rad/s in a magnetic field of 0.2 T. The peak emf generated is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega = 100\times0.2\times0.1\times50 = 100$ V.
questions.trick: AC generator peak emf: $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega$ — multiply all four factors directly.

questions.q: A bar magnet is dropped, north pole down, through a horizontal conducting loop. As the magnet approaches the loop from above, the induced current in the loop (viewed from above) is
options: clockwise, to oppose the increasing downward flux
clockwise, to aid the flux increase
anticlockwise, to oppose the increasing downward flux
questions.explanation: As the magnet approaches, downward flux through the loop increases; by Lenz's law the induced current flows anticlockwise (viewed from above the falling magnet's side) to create an opposing upward field.
questions.trick: Approaching magnet increases flux; induced current always opposes — apply Lenz's law, then right-hand rule.

questions.q: Eddy currents in a transformer core are minimised by
options: using a laminated core of thin insulated sheets
using a hollow core with no material
questions.explanation: Laminating the core into thin sheets insulated from each other increases resistance to eddy current paths, reducing eddy current (heating) losses without affecting the main flux.
questions.trick: Laminating the core (thin insulated sheets) is THE standard fix for eddy current loss.

questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.5 H. If the current in the primary changes at the rate of 4 A/s, the emf induced in the secondary is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon_2 = M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt} = 0.5\times4 = 2$ V.
questions.trick: $\varepsilon_2=M\,dI_1/dt$ — direct multiplication, ignore turns in secondary explicitly.

questions.q: A circular coil of area $0.02$ m$^2$ is placed with its plane perpendicular to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. If the field is reduced to zero uniformly in 0.1 s, the average induced emf (single turn) is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon = \Delta\phi/\Delta t = (BA)/\Delta t = (0.5\times0.02)/0.1 = 0.01/0.1 = 0.1$ V.
questions.trick: $\varepsilon=\Delta(BA)/\Delta t$ when area is fixed and field changes — same formula, swapped variable.

questions.q: The direction of induced current in a circuit is given by
questions.explanation: Lenz's law specifies the direction: the induced current opposes the change in flux causing it.
questions.trick: Direction of induced current = Lenz's law; magnitude = Faraday's law — know which does what.

questions.q: A coil is rotated in a uniform magnetic field about an axis perpendicular to the field. The induced emf is maximum when the plane of the coil is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon = -d\phi/dt = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$ is maximum when $\sin\omega t=1$, i.e. when flux $\phi=NBA\cos\omega t$ is zero — which happens when the coil plane is parallel to the field (flux through it is zero but changing fastest).
questions.trick: Emf max when flux is ZERO but changing fastest — coil plane parallel to field, not perpendicular.

questions.q: Two coils, A and B, have self-inductances $L_1$ and $L_2$ and no flux leakage (coupling coefficient $k=1$). Their mutual inductance is
questions.explanation: $M = k\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; for perfect coupling $k=1$, $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}$.
questions.trick: Perfect coupling ($k=1$): $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ — geometric mean of the two inductances.

questions.q: A metallic disc is used to demonstrate electromagnetic damping by swinging it into a magnetic field between the poles of a strong magnet. It slows down quickly mainly due to
options: eddy currents dissipating kinetic energy as heat
questions.explanation: As the disc enters/exits the field, changing flux induces eddy currents in it; the opposing force (Lenz's law) does negative work, converting kinetic energy to heat and slowing the disc.
questions.trick: Swinging disc into a field slows via eddy currents converting KE to heat — Lenz's law braking.

questions.q: The unit of self-inductance, the henry, is equivalent to
questions.explanation: From $\varepsilon=-L\,dI/dt$, $L$ has unit V/(A/s) = V s/A, defined as the henry.
questions.trick: Henry $=$ V$\cdot$s/A, from $\varepsilon=-L\,dI/dt$ — rearrange units directly.

questions.q: A square loop of side 10 cm is pulled out of a uniform magnetic field region of 0.5 T at a constant velocity of 2 m/s, with one side always inside the field boundary. The emf induced while the loop is exiting is
questions.explanation: Only the side crossing the boundary contributes: $\varepsilon = Bvl = 0.5\times2\times0.1 = 0.1$ V.
questions.trick: Only the side crossing the field boundary generates emf: $\varepsilon=Bvl$ for that side alone.

questions.q: In an AC generator, doubling the frequency of rotation (keeping $N$, $B$, $A$ fixed) causes the peak emf to
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$; since $\omega = 2\pi f$, doubling $f$ doubles $\omega$ and hence doubles $\varepsilon_0$.
questions.trick: $\varepsilon_0=NBA\omega\propto f$: doubling frequency directly doubles peak emf.

questions.q: A copper ring is held horizontally and a bar magnet is dropped vertically through it. Compared to free fall, the magnet's acceleration while passing near the ring is
options: less than $g$, due to the retarding force from induced eddy currents
questions.explanation: The changing flux induces a current in the ring which, by Lenz's law, opposes the magnet's motion, providing an upward retarding force so the net acceleration is less than $g$.
questions.trick: Falling magnet through a ring: eddy currents oppose motion, so acceleration is always $<g$.

questions.q: The electric field induced by a time-varying magnetic field differs from an electrostatic field in that it
options: has closed field lines and is non-conservative
questions.explanation: An induced electric field forms closed loops around the region of changing flux and does non-zero work around a closed path, unlike the conservative, radial electrostatic field of charges.
questions.trick: Induced E-field forms closed loops (non-conservative) — unlike electrostatic field's open radial lines.

questions.q: In an LR circuit with $L=2$ H and $R=4\,\Omega$ connected to a battery of emf 12 V, the time constant and the maximum (steady-state) current are respectively
questions.explanation: Time constant $\tau=L/R=2/4=0.5$ s; steady current $i_{max}=\varepsilon/R=12/4=3$ A.
questions.trick: LR circuit: $\tau=L/R$ and steady current $=\varepsilon/R$ — two separate, simple formulas.

questions.q: A conducting rod of length 1 m rotates about one end with angular speed 10 rad/s in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The emf induced between its ends is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon=\dfrac12B\omega l^2=\dfrac12\times0.5\times10\times1^2=2.5$ V.
questions.trick: Rotating rod: $\varepsilon=\frac12B\omega l^2$ — the extra $\frac12$ distinguishes it from linear motional emf.

questions.q: A circular loop in a uniform field 0.2 T perpendicular to its plane has radius 10 cm, expanding at $\dfrac{dr}{dt}=2$ cm/s. The instantaneous induced emf is approximately
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon = B\dfrac{dA}{dt} = B\times2\pi r\dfrac{dr}{dt} = 0.2\times2\pi\times0.1\times0.02 \approx 2.5\times10^{-3}$ V.
questions.trick: Expanding loop: $\varepsilon=B\,dA/dt=B\times2\pi r\,(dr/dt)$ — differentiate area, not radius directly.

questions.q: As an electric motor speeds up, the back emf generated in its armature
options: decreases, increasing the net current drawn
has no effect on the current
increases, reducing the net current drawn from the supply
questions.explanation: The rotating armature coil generates a back emf $\varepsilon_b$ opposing the applied voltage; as speed increases $\varepsilon_b$ increases, so the net current $i=(V-\varepsilon_b)/R$ decreases.
questions.trick: Back emf rises with motor speed, always REDUCING net current drawn — self-regulating mechanism.

questions.q: Two long coaxial solenoids of length 0.5 m and area $2\times10^{-3}$ m$^2$ have 1000 turns/m and 2000 turns/m respectively. Their mutual inductance is approximately
questions.explanation: $M=\mu_0n_1n_2Al = 4\pi\times10^{-7}\times1000\times2000\times2\times10^{-3}\times0.5 \approx 2.5\times10^{-3}$ H.
questions.trick: Coaxial solenoids: $M=\mu_0n_1n_2Al$ — use turn densities ($n=N/l$), not total turns.

questions.q: The coefficient of coupling $k$ between two coils is defined as $k = M/\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. Its value lies in the range
questions.explanation: $k=0$ means no flux linkage between coils; $k=1$ means perfect coupling (no leakage flux); $k$ cannot exceed 1.
questions.trick: Coupling coefficient $k$ always lies between 0 (no linkage) and 1 (perfect coupling).

questions.q: Two inductors of 3 H and 5 H (no mutual coupling) are connected in series. The equivalent inductance is
questions.explanation: For inductors in series with no coupling, $L=L_1+L_2=3+5=8$ H.
questions.trick: Uncoupled series inductors: just add, $L=L_1+L_2$, like series resistors.

questions.q: A straight long wire carries a steadily increasing current $I$. A conducting loop lies in the same plane, to one side of the wire. The induced current in the loop flows in a direction such that it
options: is zero, as the loop does not enclose the wire
opposes the increase in flux through it, flowing anti-parallel to $I$ in the near side
flows parallel to $I$ in the near side of the loop, reinforcing the flux
questions.explanation: The wire's increasing current increases the flux through the loop; by Lenz's law the induced current opposes this increase, flowing anti-parallel to $I$ on the side nearest the wire.
questions.trick: Increasing current nearby: induced current in loop opposes rise, flows anti-parallel on the near side.

questions.q: The phenomenon of mutual induction is used in the working of
questions.explanation: A transformer transfers energy between primary and secondary coils purely through mutual induction, with no electrical contact between them.
questions.trick: Mutual induction's classic application: the transformer, no electrical contact needed.

questions.q: In an LR circuit, at a time equal to one time constant after the switch is closed, the current reaches approximately what fraction of its final steady value?
questions.trick: LR growth: 63% of final current after one time constant — memorise $1-e^{-1}\approx0.63$.

questions.q: Two inductors of self-inductance $L$ and $4L$ carry the same current $I$. The ratio of energy stored in them (first : second) is
questions.explanation: $U=\dfrac12LI^2$; for the same $I$, $U\propto L$, so the ratio is $L:4L=1:4$.
questions.trick: $U=\frac12LI^2$, same $I$: energy ratio equals inductance ratio directly, $L:4L$.

questions.q: When the battery in an LR circuit is suddenly short-circuited (removed), after one time constant the current falls to approximately
questions.explanation: Decay follows $i=i_0e^{-t/\tau}$; at $t=\tau$, $i=i_0e^{-1}\approx0.37\,i_0$, i.e. 37%.
questions.trick: LR decay: 37% of initial current remains after one time constant ($e^{-1}\approx0.37$).

questions.q: A coil of area 0.1 m$^2$ is rotated from a position where its plane is perpendicular to a 0.4 T field to a position where its plane is parallel to the field, in 0.2 s. The average induced emf is
questions.explanation: Initial flux $\phi_1=BA=0.4\times0.1=0.04$ Wb, final flux $\phi_2=0$; average emf $=\Delta\phi/\Delta t=0.04/0.2=0.2$ V.
questions.trick: Perpendicular-to-parallel rotation: flux goes from $BA$ to zero — use $\Delta\phi/\Delta t$ directly.

questions.q: The negative sign in Faraday's law, $\varepsilon = -N\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}$, signifies that
options: current cannot flow in the coil
the induced emf opposes the change in flux producing it (Lenz's law)
questions.explanation: The negative sign encodes Lenz's law: the induced emf drives a current whose effects oppose the very change in flux that caused it, consistent with energy conservation.
questions.trick: Negative sign in Faraday's law IS Lenz's law — opposition to the flux change, always.

questions.q: A bar magnet and a coil approach each other with the same relative speed in two situations: (i) magnet fixed, coil moves; (ii) coil fixed, magnet moves. The induced emf in the coil is
options: the same in both cases, depending only on relative velocity
questions.explanation: Since only the relative motion between magnet and coil determines the rate of change of flux, the induced emf is identical in both cases for the same relative speed.
questions.trick: Only relative velocity between magnet and coil matters — emf is the same either way.

questions.q: A small circular loop of radius 2 cm lies concentrically and coplanar with a much larger loop of radius 50 cm. The mutual inductance between them is approximately (use $M=\dfrac{\mu_0\pi r^2}{2R}$)
questions.explanation: $M=\dfrac{\mu_0\pi r^2}{2R}=\dfrac{4\pi\times10^{-7}\times\pi\times(0.02)^2}{2\times0.5}\approx1.6\times10^{-9}$ H.
questions.trick: Given formula questions: just substitute values carefully, watch the powers of 10.

questions.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction is applicable to
options: only a changing magnetic field with the conductor at rest
both motional emf and emf due to a changing field with the coil at rest
questions.explanation: Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-Nd\phi/dt$, is completely general — it covers emf from a conductor moving through a field as well as emf from a purely time-varying field with a stationary coil.
questions.trick: Faraday's law covers BOTH motional emf and changing-field emf — fully general, no restriction.

questions.q: In an LR circuit connected to a battery of emf $\varepsilon$, the rate of growth of current $di/dt$ is maximum at
options: it is constant at all times
$t=0$, immediately after closing the switch, equal to $\varepsilon/L$
questions.explanation: From $\varepsilon=L\,di/dt+iR$, at $t=0$, $i=0$, so $di/dt=\varepsilon/L$, its maximum value; as current builds up, $di/dt$ decreases towards zero.
questions.trick: $di/dt$ is maximum at $t=0$ (equals $\varepsilon/L$) and decreases as current builds up.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Eddy currents are used for electromagnetic braking in trains and roller-coasters. Reason (R): Eddy currents dissipate kinetic energy as heat, providing a smooth, contact-free braking force. Choose the correct option.
options: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.explanation: As the moving conductor enters/exits a magnetic field, induced eddy currents oppose the motion (Lenz's law) and convert kinetic energy into heat, giving smooth braking without mechanical contact.
questions.trick: Eddy currents brake by converting KE to heat via Lenz's law — contact-free, smooth deceleration.
